questions.question: How does the kubelet communicate with the container runtime on a node?
options: Through the Docker Engine API directly
Through the CRI (Container Runtime Interface), using runtimes such as containerd or CRI-O
By exec'ing into the runtime container manually
Through the etcd storage backend
questions.explanation: The kubelet talks to runtimes via the CRI gRPC interface. The built-in Docker support (dockershim) was removed in Kubernetes v1.24, so CRI-compatible runtimes like containerd and CRI-O are used instead.

questions.question: Which Kubernetes component is the central control-plane entry point that exposes the Kubernetes API?
options: kube-scheduler
kube-apiserver
etcd
kube-controller-manager
questions.explanation: The kube-apiserver is the front end for the control plane: it authenticates, authorizes, and validates all API requests, and is the only component that talks directly to etcd.

questions.question: Where does a Kubernetes cluster persist its entire state and configuration?
options: In the kube-apiserver memory only
In etcd, the distributed key-value store
In a SQLite database on the master node
In ConfigMaps on every worker node
questions.explanation: etcd is the cluster's source of truth - a consistent distributed key-value store. Every object, from Pods to RBAC rules, is persisted there via the API server.

questions.question: What is the smallest deployable unit that Kubernetes manages?
options: A container image
A Pod
A Deployment
A node
questions.explanation: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more tightly coupled containers sharing network and storage, scheduled together onto a node.

questions.question: A Pod has no nodeSelector or affinity rules. Which component decides which node it runs on?
options: The kubelet on each node
The kube-scheduler
The cloud-controller-manager
The kube-apiserver
questions.explanation: The kube-scheduler watches for unscheduled Pods and assigns them to nodes based on resource availability, taints/tolerations, affinity, and topology constraints. The kubelet then starts the Pod locally.

questions.question: Which kubectl command lists Pods across ALL namespaces?
options: kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
kubectl get pods --recursive
kubectl get pods -n default
questions.explanation: The -n/--namespace flag selects a namespace, and --all-namespaces (short -A) widens the query to every namespace. -o wide only adds extra output columns.

questions.question: What is the primary responsibility of the kubelet?
options: Routing traffic between Services
Acting as the node agent that ensures containers described in Pod specs are running and healthy
Resolving cluster DNS queries
Provisioning persistent volumes
questions.explanation: The kubelet runs on every node and is responsible for receiving Pod specs from the API server, starting/stopping containers via the runtime, and reporting node and Pod status.

questions.question: Which Service type exposes the Service on a port on every node's IP address?
options: ClusterIP
NodePort
LoadBalancer
ExternalName
questions.explanation: A NodePort service opens a port on every node and forwards external traffic to the backing Pods. ClusterIP is internal-only, LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer, and ExternalName is a DNS CNAME alias.

questions.question: What does a Deployment manage directly?
options: A ReplicaSet, which in turn manages the Pods
The Pods directly, without any intermediate object
The nodes the Pods run on
The Service routing rules
questions.explanation: Deployments own ReplicaSets. The Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet during a rollout, while the ReplicaSet ensures the desired number of Pods exist.

questions.question: Which Kubernetes object is designed to store sensitive data such as passwords and TLS keys?
options: ConfigMap
Secret
PersistentVolumeClaim
ServiceAccount
questions.explanation: Secrets store and inject sensitive data (base64-encoded, with encryption at rest if configured). ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration, PVCs request storage, and ServiceAccounts identify processes within the cluster.

questions.question: What is the default type of a Kubernetes Service?
options: NodePort
ClusterIP
LoadBalancer
Headless
questions.explanation: Services default to ClusterIP, which exposes the Service on an internal virtual IP reachable only within the cluster. You must explicitly request NodePort or LoadBalancer.

questions.question: Which resource object is used to define HTTP/HTTPS routing rules such as hostnames and path-based routing?
options: Ingress
NetworkPolicy
Endpoint
CustomResourceDefinition
questions.explanation: An Ingress object defines HTTP(S) routing rules (hosts, paths, TLS) and is fulfilled by an Ingress controller such as ingress-nginx. NetworkPolicies control traffic allow/deny, not routing.

questions.question: How does a Service find the Pods it routes traffic to?
options: By matching Pod names listed in an endpoint file
By its label selector matching the labels on Pods
By the namespace the Pods belong to
By the node the Pods run on
questions.explanation: A Service has a selector (e.g. spec.selector: { app: web }) that matches Pod labels. The endpoints controller continuously updates the Endpoints/EndpointSlice object with the IPs of matching Pods.

questions.question: What is a PersistentVolume (PV)?
options: A piece of storage in the cluster, provisioned by an admin or dynamically, that outlives individual Pods
A directory on the node that is recreated when the Pod restarts
A cache directory inside a container
A replica of etcd storage
questions.explanation: A PV is a cluster-level storage resource with a lifecycle independent of any Pod. Pods consume storage indirectly through PersistentVolumeClaims.

questions.question: What does a StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer do?
options: Binds the PersistentVolumeClaim immediately when it is created
Delays binding until a Pod using the claim is scheduled, so the volume can be placed in the right zone
Deletes the claim when the Pod stops using it
Converts the volume to a hostPath mount
questions.explanation: WaitForFirstConsumer defers volume binding until a consumer Pod is scheduled, which avoids cross-zone volume attachment issues and enables topology-aware provisioning.

questions.question: Which workload controller runs a Pod to successful completion exactly once (e.g. a batch job)?
options: Deployment
Job
DaemonSet
StatefulSet
questions.explanation: A Job runs Pods until they complete successfully, retrying on failure. Deployments keep Pods running forever, DaemonSets run one Pod per node, and StatefulSets manage identity-bound long-running Pods.

questions.question: Which workload controller guarantees that exactly one Pod of a given template runs on every node in the cluster?
options: DaemonSet
StatefulSet
Deployment
ReplicaSet
questions.explanation: DaemonSets ensure one Pod per node (including nodes added later). They are commonly used for node agents such as log collectors and monitoring exporters.

questions.question: What is the purpose of taints and tolerations?
options: To attract specific Pods to a node
To repel Pods from a node unless the Pod explicitly tolerates the taint
To balance Pods across availability zones
To limit how much CPU a Pod may use
questions.explanation: A taint on a node repels Pods that don't tolerate it (e.g. the built-in node.kubernetes.io/not-ready taint). Tolerations in a Pod spec allow it to be scheduled onto tainted nodes.

questions.question: What does kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml do?
options: Creates the resources imperatively and never updates them afterwards
Declaratively creates or updates resources so the cluster matches the file's desired state
Deletes everything defined in the file
Validates the file without contacting the API server
questions.explanation: kubectl apply is the declarative approach: it sends the manifest to the API server, creating or updating the object (adding the last-applied-configuration annotation for three-way diffs).

questions.question: Which API group and version should be used for a Deployment in a current Kubernetes cluster?
options: extensions/v1beta1
apps/v1beta2
apps/v1
v1
questions.explanation: Deployments are GA under apps/v1. The legacy extensions/v1beta1 and apps/v1beta2 APIs were deprecated and removed - deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets, and replicasets all live in the apps/v1 group.

questions.question: What is a namespace in Kubernetes?
options: A physical hardware partition of the cluster
A virtual partition within a single cluster for logically isolating related resources
A separate Kubernetes cluster
A network segment with its own IP range
questions.explanation: Namespaces provide virtual isolation inside one cluster - useful for separating environments or teams and for scoping resource quotas and RBAC. They do not provide hard network or hardware isolation.

questions.question: What does kube-proxy do on each node?
options: Resolves Service DNS names
Programs networking rules (iptables or IPVS) so Service virtual IPs reach the correct Pods
Schedules Pods onto the node
Stores the cluster state in etcd
questions.explanation: kube-proxy maintains the node's networking rules so traffic to a Service's virtual IP is load-balanced to the matching Pod endpoints. Cluster DNS is handled by CoreDNS, not kube-proxy.

questions.question: In a Pod spec, what does imagePullPolicy: Never instruct the kubelet to do?
options: Always pull the latest image from the registry
Use only an image already present on the node; never contact a registry
Pull the image once and cache it forever
Pull the image only from a private registry
questions.explanation: imagePullPolicy: Never means the kubelet must find the image locally on the node, otherwise the container fails to start (ErrImageNeverPull). This is common in air-gapped or preloaded-node setups.

questions.question: What is the difference between a container's resource requests and limits?
options: Requests are the maximum the container may use; limits are the guaranteed minimum
Requests are the minimum guaranteed amount used for scheduling; limits are the maximum the container may consume
Requests are for CPU only; limits apply only to memory
There is no difference - they are interchangeable fields
questions.explanation: requests define the minimum guaranteed resources (used by the scheduler to place the Pod); limits define the hard ceiling - exceeding the memory limit kills the container (OOMKilled), while exceeding the CPU limit throttles it.

questions.question: How do you ensure a Pod is only scheduled onto nodes with a specific label, such as disk=ssd?
options: Set a nodeSelector in the Pod spec matching the node label
Add an annotation to the Service
Create a ResourceQuota in the namespace
Taint every other namespace
questions.explanation: A nodeSelector (e.g. nodeSelector: { disk: ssd }) constrains scheduling to nodes carrying that label. For more expressive rules (set-based matching, preferred rules), use node affinity.

questions.question: How does kubectl describe pod differ from kubectl logs?
options: kubectl describe shows object details and recent events; kubectl logs shows the output of the container process
They are identical commands
kubectl describe shows only logs; kubectl logs shows only events
kubectl describe works offline; kubectl logs requires the API server
questions.explanation: kubectl describe renders the full object spec plus status and the last events from the namespace - invaluable for diagnosing scheduling and probe failures - while kubectl logs streams the container's stdout/stderr.

questions.question: What is the default update strategy of a Kubernetes Deployment?
options: RollingUpdate
Recreate
Blue-green
Canary
questions.explanation: Deployments default to RollingUpdate, gradually replacing old Pods with new ones while respecting maxUnavailable and maxSurge. Recreate must be requested explicitly; blue-green and canary are application-level patterns built on top of Kubernetes primitives.

questions.question: During a Deployment rollout, what does maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 accomplish?
options: Pauses the rollout until an operator resumes it
Never drops below the desired replica count - it creates one extra Pod first and removes old Pods only once new ones are ready
Deletes all old Pods before starting new ones
Limits the rollout to one node
questions.explanation: maxUnavailable: 0 keeps every replica available throughout the rollout, while maxSurge: 1 allows one extra Pod to be created temporarily. The result is a zero-downtime update.

questions.question: A Pod managed by a Deployment is deleted. What causes it to be replaced?
options: The kube-scheduler detects the missing Pod
The ReplicaSet controller notices the current replica count is below the desired count and creates a new Pod
The kubelet on the node restarts the container
The Ingress controller reschedules it
questions.explanation: Each Deployment owns a ReplicaSet that continuously reconciles: if live Pods fall below the replicas field, it creates more. The scheduler only places already-created Pods; it doesn't create them.

questions.question: What does kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5 do?
options: Increases the CPU limit on the web Pods to 5 cores
Updates the Deployment's replicas field so the ReplicaSet creates or removes Pods to reach 5
Creates 5 separate Deployments named web
Scales the underlying node count to 5
questions.explanation: Scaling changes the desired replica count in the Deployment spec. The ReplicaSet controller then adds or deletes Pods to converge on that number.

questions.question: What drives the decisions of a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)?
options: The number of nodes in the cluster
Observed metrics such as CPU or memory utilization compared to a target value
The time of day
The number of etcd keys
questions.explanation: The HPA periodically samples metrics (CPU/memory from metrics-server, or custom/external metrics) and scales replicas so the observed utilization matches the target. It scales horizontally (more Pods), not vertically.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a readiness probe?
options: To restart a container that has crashed
To determine whether the container is ready to accept traffic - until it passes, the Pod's IP is excluded from Service endpoints
To measure how long the container took to start
To terminate the container when memory is exhausted
questions.explanation: A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints so no traffic is sent until the application is actually able to serve. Liveness probes, by contrast, trigger container restarts.

questions.question: What happens when a liveness probe fails repeatedly?
options: The Pod is removed from the Service endpoints only
The container is killed and restarted by the kubelet according to the restart policy
The Pod is rescheduled onto another node immediately
The rollout is automatically rolled back
questions.explanation: Liveness failures cause the kubelet to restart the container (the classic fix for deadlocked or hung applications). To avoid the same fate during startup, use a startup probe. Readiness failures only divert traffic.

questions.question: Why would you add a startup probe to a container?
options: To speed up the startup of slow applications
To give a slow-starting application time to initialize without the liveness probe killing it
To replace the readiness probe entirely
To probe the node's health
questions.explanation: A startup probe runs until it succeeds, and liveness/readiness probes don't begin until it passes. This protects applications that need a long initialization period from being restarted by an impatient liveness probe.

questions.question: Which workload controller should be used for a database that needs a stable network identity and stable persistent storage across restarts?
options: Deployment
DaemonSet
StatefulSet
Job
questions.explanation: StatefulSets provide stable, ordinal pod names (mysql-0, mysql-1...), stable DNS names, and per-pod PersistentVolumeClaims - exactly what stateful workloads like databases need.

questions.question: In a Helm chart, what is the purpose of values.yaml?
options: It documents the chart's license
It provides default configuration values that users can override at install/upgrade time
It lists the cluster's nodes
It stores Secrets in plain text
questions.explanation: values.yaml holds the chart's default configuration. Users override these values (via -f files or --set flags) to customize an installation without editing the templates.

questions.question: What is a Helm release?
options: A new version of the Kubernetes API
A single installed instance of a chart, with its own name, history, and state
The container image tag of an application
A Helm repository URL
questions.explanation: Every helm install creates a release - a named, tracked instance of a chart. You can upgrade, roll back (helm rollback), or uninstall releases independently, and Helm stores their history in the cluster.

questions.question: What does helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart do?
options: Always creates a duplicate installation alongside the existing one
Installs the chart if the release doesn't exist, otherwise upgrades the existing release in place - making it safe for CI pipelines
Downgrades Kubernetes itself
Uninstalls the release before reinstalling it
questions.explanation: The --install flag makes the command idempotent: it installs when absent and upgrades when present. This one-liner is the standard pattern for automated continuous delivery pipelines.

questions.question: What is the effect of a ResourceQuota on a namespace?
options: It limits the number of namespaces a user can create
It caps the total amount of compute resources (or object counts) that all objects in the namespace may request
It quarantines a namespace during incidents
It reserves resources exclusively for the namespace on every node
questions.explanation: ResourceQuotas enforce ceilings per namespace - e.g. a maximum total CPU/memory or maximum number of Pods - which is the standard way to stop one team or environment from consuming the whole cluster.

questions.question: Which component provides the resource usage data (CPU/memory) that kubectl top and the HPA rely on?
options: etcd
metrics-server
kube-proxy
CoreDNS
questions.explanation: metrics-server collects resource usage metrics from the kubelets on each node and exposes them via the metrics API. Without it, kubectl top fails and CPU/memory-based HPAs cannot function.

questions.question: Which type of probe simply checks whether a TCP connection to a container's port succeeds?
options: HTTP GET probe
TCP socket probe
exec probe
liveness probe
questions.explanation: A TCP probe opens a socket to the specified port and succeeds if the connection is established. HTTP probes check for a successful status code; exec probes run a command inside the container.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)?
options: To prevent a node from running too many Pods
To limit how many Pods may be voluntarily disrupted at once (e.g. during node drains or cluster upgrades) so the application stays available
To set CPU and memory budgets for a Pod
To reserve budget for future node autoscaling
questions.explanation: A PDB guards against voluntary disruptions: cluster upgrades and kubectl drain will respect it and only evict as many Pods as allowed. It does not protect against node failures or crashes (involuntary disruptions).

questions.question: You run kubectl rollout status deployment/web. What are you checking?
options: The rollout history of the Deployment
Whether the in-progress rollout has completed and all new Pods are available
The resource usage of the new Pods
Whether the Deployment's image was pulled successfully
questions.explanation: rollout status watches the live state of a rollout and reports when the new ReplicaSet has reached the desired, available replicas - commonly used to gate CI/CD pipelines on successful deployments.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of Continuous Integration (CI)?
options: To deploy directly to production on every commit
To integrate and verify developers' changes frequently and automatically so integration problems are found early
To write documentation continuously
To replace manual code reviews
questions.explanation: CI means merging changes into a shared mainline many times a day, with every merge automatically built and tested. The payoff is early detection of integration defects, not automatic production deployment.

questions.question: What is the core principle of GitOps?
options: Developers push changes directly to production clusters with kubectl
Git is the single source of truth for the desired state, and automated agents reconcile the cluster to match it
Every deployment requires manually merging pull requests on the cluster
Git repositories are hosted inside the Kubernetes cluster
questions.explanation: In GitOps the desired state of the system lives in Git; an agent (Argo CD or Flux) continuously compares the actual cluster state with the repo and applies differences. This gives auditability, rollback via git revert, and self-healing.

questions.question: Which of these is a CNCF Graduated GitOps continuous-delivery tool that reconciles Kubernetes clusters with manifests in Git?
options: Jenkins
Argo CD
Travis CI
SonarQube
questions.explanation: Argo CD (CNCF Graduated) is a declarative GitOps CD tool for Kubernetes. Jenkins and Travis CI are general CI systems (push-based), and SonarQube is a code-quality platform.

questions.question: In a push-based CI/CD pipeline versus a GitOps (pull-based) model, what is the key difference?
options: Push-based requires Git; GitOps does not use Git
In GitOps, the in-cluster agent pulls the desired state from Git - the CI system never needs cluster credentials
Pull-based is slower because humans apply the changes
There is no practical difference; only the naming changed
questions.explanation: With GitOps, reconciliation is pulled from inside the cluster by an agent, so the CI pipeline doesn't need kubernetes secrets or direct cluster access - a smaller credential blast radius plus a full audit trail in Git.

questions.question: What is progressive delivery?
options: Deploying to production progressively over several weeks without metrics
Gradually rolling out a new version to a small slice of users, measuring key metrics, and expanding only if the metrics stay healthy
Shipping features one file at a time
Deploying each microservice to its own cluster
questions.explanation: Progressive delivery (canary releases, feature flags, automated analysis) limits the blast radius of a release and uses live metrics as a gate before full rollout - with automatic rollback when signals degrade.

questions.question: What is the defining characteristic of a blue-green deployment?
options: Traffic is gradually shifted by percentage
Two full environments (old and new) run side by side, and traffic switches between them atomically - rollback means switching back
Only two microservices are ever deployed
The database schema is never migrated
questions.explanation: Blue-green keeps two identical environments and flips a single switch (e.g. a Service selector or Ingress weight) from the old version to the new one. Instant rollback is the main benefit; the cost is running double capacity.

questions.question: How does a canary release work?
options: All users get the new version at once, then it is rolled back if issues appear
A small percentage of traffic is routed to the new version while most users stay on the old one; metrics determine expansion or rollback
The new version is only released on weekends
Two clusters are kept permanently in sync
questions.explanation: A canary exposes only a small slice of traffic to the new version first. If error rates or latency stay healthy, the rollout expands; if not, traffic returns to the stable version with minimal impact.

questions.question: What does the principle of immutable infrastructure mean?
options: Servers must never be patched or rebooted
Instead of modifying running servers or containers in place, you build new images/artifacts and replace instances
All data must be stored in read-only volumes
Infrastructure objects cannot be deleted once created
questions.explanation: Immutable infrastructure means replacing rather than patching in place: build a new container image, roll it out, discard the old instances. This eliminates configuration drift and makes rollbacks trivial and reliable.

questions.question: What is the role of an artifact registry in a cloud native delivery pipeline?
options: To compile source code into binaries
To store versioned, immutable artifacts such as container images and Helm charts so deployments are reproducible
To monitor running applications
To manage developer identities
questions.explanation: A registry (e.g. Harbor, ECR, GHCR) stores versioned container images and charts. Deployments reference immutable digests, giving reproducibility, provenance, and a place to run vulnerability scans before promotion.

questions.question: What does Infrastructure as Code (IaC) mean?
options: Writing application logic inside VM images
Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable definitions stored in version control, applied repeatably and automatically
Manually clicking through a cloud provider's web console
Compiling infrastructure into container images
questions.explanation: IaC expresses infrastructure (networks, clusters, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform configs) as versioned declarative definitions. This makes environments reproducible, reviewable via pull requests, and recoverable.

questions.question: According to the CNCF, what best describes a cloud native application?
options: Any application hosted on a public cloud vendor's servers
An application built from loosely coupled, resilient, manageable, observable microservices, packaged in containers and managed by agile processes
An application written exclusively in Go
A monolithic application deployed on Kubernetes
questions.explanation: The CNCF defines cloud native as using loosely coupled, resilient, manageable, observable microservices, typically containerized and orchestrated (Kubernetes), supported by agile infrastructure and delivery practices.

questions.question: In the twelve-factor app methodology, where should configuration that varies between deployments (credentials, URLs) be stored?
options: Hard-coded in the source code
In environment variables (or config injected via the environment)
In the container image
On a shared network drive
questions.explanation: Factor III (Config) says strict separation of config from code: store environment-specific values in the environment (in Kubernetes, injected via ConfigMaps and Secrets), so the same build runs unchanged across dev, staging, and prod.

questions.question: What is the difference between declarative and imperative APIs?
options: Declarative APIs tell the system HOW to do each step; imperative APIs state the desired END STATE
Declarative APIs state the desired end state and the system works out how to achieve it; imperative APIs specify each action to perform
They are the same concept with different names
Declarative APIs only work with YAML; imperative APIs only work with JSON
questions.explanation: Kubernetes is declarative: you submit the desired state (a Pod spec) and controllers continuously reconcile toward it. Imperative commands (kubectl create/run) specify individual actions with no ongoing reconciliation.

questions.question: What does a service mesh provide?
options: A physical cable between microservices
Infrastructure-level traffic management, security (mTLS), and observability between services, without changing application code
A replacement for the Kubernetes control plane
A container image build system
questions.explanation: A service mesh (e.g. Istio, Linkerd) adds a sidecar-based layer that handles service-to-service traffic (routing, retries, circuit breaking), mutual TLS, and telemetry - independently of application code and language.

questions.question: What are the three commonly cited pillars of observability?
options: Metrics, logs, and traces
CPU, memory, and disk
Alerts, dashboards, and reports
Events, audits, and dumps
questions.explanation: Metrics (numeric time series), logs (discrete event records), and traces (request paths across services) together make a system's internal state understandable from the outside - the standard observability triad.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the circuit breaker pattern in a microservices architecture?
options: To physically cut power to failing services
To stop calls to a failing service after repeated failures, preventing cascading failures across the system and giving it time to recover
To encrypt traffic between services
To balance traffic evenly regardless of service health
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker 'opens' after a failure threshold, failing fast instead of hammering a struggling dependency. This stops timeouts from cascading through callers; it then half-opens to test whether the service has recovered.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of a microservices architecture over a monolith?
options: Microservices always require less total code
Each service can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently, so teams can ship and scale parts of the system separately
Microservices eliminate the need for APIs
A single deployment pipeline covers the entire system
questions.explanation: Microservices trade deployment complexity for independence: teams own services end-to-end, deploy on their own cadence, and scale hot components independently. The costs - network boundaries, distributed data, eventual consistency - are the trade-off.
